name: Parkinson's Law of Triviality
statement: The time a committee spends on an item is inversely proportional to the money involved.
statementAccent: inversely proportional to the money involved
meaning: Groups devote disproportionate time and energy to small, familiar, easy-to-grasp matters while waving through the genuinely important, costly, and complex ones. Effort is allocated in inverse proportion to actual stakes.
mechanism: People weigh in on what they understand and feel qualified to judge. A multi-million-pound reactor is too technical for the average committee member to engage with, so they defer and approve it quickly. A bicycle shed is within everyone's comprehension — everyone can picture one — so everyone has an opinion and wants to leave a mark, and the trivial item swallows the meeting.

examples.text: Parkinson's original: a finance committee approves a £10 million atomic reactor in about two and a half minutes (too big to grasp), argues for three-quarters of an hour over a £350 bicycle shed, and spends over an hour on a £21-a-year refreshment budget — the smallest sum drawing the longest fight.

In 1999 the FreeBSD developer Poul-Henning Kamp, exasperated by an endless mailing-list thread, wrote 'A bike shed (any colour will do)…', popularising 'bikeshedding' for teams that agonise over trivia while real design decisions pass unexamined.

The everyday form: a group nods through a large budget or a strategy in minutes, then debates the logo colour, the office snacks, or the meeting time at length — the parts everyone feels entitled to judge.

variants.name: Bikeshedding
variants.text: The software world's name for the same law, from Kamp's 1999 email: the urge to argue about the colour of the bike shed — the thing anyone can build over a weekend — rather than the reactor no one dares question.

variants.name: Sayre's law
variants.text: The close relative: in any dispute the intensity of feeling is inversely proportional to the value of the issues at stake — which is why the trivial agenda item generates the most heat.

whyItMatters: It explains a universal failure of meetings: the cheap, comprehensible item crowds out the expensive, consequential one, because scrutiny follows understanding rather than importance. Naming it lets a chair defend the decisions that matter from the ones everyone can weigh in on.

working.lead: Put a clock on the trivial
working.text: timebox cheap, easily-understood items so they cannot expand to fill the meeting; the bike shed does not deserve the reactor's hour.
deliberately allocate the most time and the most expert attention to the biggest, most complex decisions — the ones that will otherwise be nodded through.
when a topic draws unusually broad participation, check whether it is drawing that energy because it matters or merely because it is easy to picture.

limits: It began as satire, not measurement — the figures and timings are an illustrative anecdote, not data — and it is a caricature: real decision processes vary, and some apparently 'trivial' debates (a product name, a UI colour, a policy's wording) genuinely matter. It is nonetheless a widely-recognised organisational tendency with strong face validity. It is best read as a sharp observation about attention, not a quantified law.
misreadings: It is not a claim that small things never matter, nor a licence to skip discussion of details. It is the observation that groups systematically over-weight the trivial because it is comprehensible — a prompt to ration attention by stakes, not by how easy something is to have an opinion about.
origin: Stated by C. Northcote Parkinson in his 1957 book Parkinson's Law, or The Pursuit of Progress, in the essay 'High Finance, or the Point of Vanishing Interest' — a different essay from, and not to be confused with, his main law that work expands to fill the time available. The software term 'bikeshedding' comes from Poul-Henning Kamp's 1999 FreeBSD email.
